title: Kevin Warsh Just Finished His First Week as Fed Chair. Markets Are Already Betting He Will Be Forced to Raise Rates.
excerpt: Warsh was sworn in promising lower rates. But inflation at 3.8 per cent, oil prices 30 per cent above pre-war levels, and a nine-week stock rally have left him with almost no room to deliver. NRI investors face a June of dual central bank risk.
body:
Kevin Warsh completed his first week as Federal Reserve Chair on Friday. He inherited the job promising to lower interest rates. The market is now pricing the opposite.

Futures contracts show a 47 per cent probability that rates will be unchanged through the end of 2026, and a 39 per cent chance they will be a quarter-point higher. The probability of a rate cut this year has collapsed to 0.6 per cent. The Atlanta Fed Market Probability Tracker confirms what bond traders have already priced in: the next move, when it comes, is far more likely to be up than down.

The Numbers That Changed the Conversation

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure — rose 3.8 per cent year-over-year in April, the highest reading since May 2023. Core PCE, which strips out food and energy, decelerated slightly to 0.2 per cent month-over-month, but the headline number is what matters politically and psychologically.

The driver is energy. Crude oil prices remain roughly 30 per cent above pre-war levels, a direct consequence of the three-month US-Israeli conflict with Iran that has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. A draft agreement to extend the ceasefire for 60 days sent oil prices down 1.6 per cent on Friday, but analysts warn that even if the strait reopens, physical damage to Gulf infrastructure and depleted inventories will keep prices elevated for months.

"Even if oil prices fall, we won't see a quick return to the pre-war inflation picture," said Steven Blitz, chief US economist at TS Lombard. "The switch from cutting to hiking is a big decision for the Fed, as it starts them and the market on a new pricing path."

Warsh Faces a Divided FOMC

Warsh's first Federal Open Market Committee meeting is scheduled for 16-17 June. At the last FOMC meeting under Jerome Powell, three governors dissented on the dovish side, signalling appetite for cuts even as inflation re-accelerated. The incoming chair inherits a committee that does not agree on direction, at a moment when the data does not offer a clean answer.

Markets widely expect rates to be held steady at the June meeting. But the forward guidance — what Warsh says about the path ahead — will be scrutinised more intensely than any rate decision.

"I think this is a test for the new chair," said James Bullard, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis. "Markets always test the new chair. They're trying to find out how will this person react in different situations."

The concern is not just economic. Warsh was appointed by President Donald Trump, who has publicly and repeatedly demanded lower interest rates. There is a nagging worry in bond markets that Warsh cannot act independently of the White House — that he was chosen not for his monetary policy expertise, but for his willingness to cut. If inflation forces him to hike instead, the credibility test will be severe.

The S&P 500 Has Rallied for Nine Straight Weeks

Against this backdrop, US equity markets have been remarkably buoyant. The S&P 500 posted its ninth consecutive weekly gain, climbing more than 10 per cent on the year. The Nasdaq Composite is up 16 per cent. Goldman Sachs raised its year-end S&P 500 target from 7,600 to 8,000, citing strong corporate earnings.

Technology stocks have led the charge. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index has jumped roughly 80 per cent since the March low. Broadcom, now the sixth-largest US company by market capitalisation, reports earnings on 4 June and could set the tone for the AI trade heading into summer.

But the rally is vulnerable. Treasury yields have eased modestly — the 10-year is around 4.45 per cent — but remain nearly 50 basis points above pre-war levels. Some models suggest yields are approaching the threshold where equities begin to suffer.

"If you saw a real spike in interest rates that was maintained, that would be the thing that I think would be most disconcerting for investors," said Chuck Carlson, CEO at Horizon Investment Services.

NRI Investors Face a Dual Central Bank Month

For investors with exposure to both US and Indian markets, June is uniquely consequential.

The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee meets from 3 to 5 June. A Reuters poll of 56 economists found that 44 expect the RBI to hold the repo rate at 5.25 per cent, but 11 now forecast a 25-basis-point hike — up from just one respondent in the April poll.

India's retail inflation remains below the RBI's 4 per cent target at 3.48 per cent, but wholesale inflation has accelerated sharply, the rupee has fallen roughly 6 per cent this year, and the monsoon forecast has deteriorated. Governor Sanjay Malhotra announces the decision on 5 June — the same day the US jobs report is released.

May non-farm payrolls are expected to show 96,000 jobs added, with unemployment at 4.3 per cent. A strong number could reignite rate-hike fears. A weak number could raise recession worries. Either outcome feeds volatility.

For NRI investors holding both dollar- and rupee-denominated assets, the sequencing matters. A Fed that leans hawkish while the RBI holds steady would widen the interest rate differential, putting further pressure on the rupee and potentially accelerating capital outflows from Indian equities. India's MSCI Emerging Markets weighting has already halved from 20 per cent to 11 per cent, and foreign investors pulled $24 billion from Indian markets in May alone.

The month ahead requires attention to two central banks, two currencies, and one war that refuses to end cleanly.

---

Sources: Reuters, MarketWatch, Morningstar, Barron's, Motley Fool, FXStreet (DBS Research), Outlook Money, Livemint, CME FedWatch Tool
nri_angle: NRI investors with both dollar and rupee holdings face a uniquely dangerous June. The RBI decides on June 5 and the Fed on June 16-17. A hawkish Fed with a steady RBI would widen the rate differential, pressure the rupee, and accelerate capital outflows from Indian equities. India's MSCI EM weight has already halved to 11 per cent.
author: Diaspora Desk
